 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman" ALIGN="center"><B><A NAME="tx807896_1"></A>EXPLANATORY NOTE </B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Adams Street Credit Solutions Fund is filing this registration statement on Form 10 (the &#8220;<B>Registration Statement</B>&#8221;) with the
Securities and Exchange Commission (the &#8220;<B>SEC</B>&#8221;) under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as amended (the &#8220;<B>1934 Act</B>&#8221;), in connection with its election to be regulated as a business development company
(&#8220;<B>BDC</B>&#8221;) under the Investment Company Act of 1940, as amended (the &#8220;<B>1940 Act</B>&#8221;), and to provide current public information to the investment community while conducting a private offering of securities. </P>

<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">This Registration Statement does not constitute an offer to sell, or the solicitation of an offer to buy, within the meaning of the 1933 Act,
any beneficial interests of the Company or any other Adams Street affiliated entity. Upon the effective date of this Registration Statement, the Company will be subject to the requirements of Section&nbsp;13(a) of the 1934 Act, including the rules
and regulations promulgated under the 1934 Act, which will require the Company to file annual reports on Form <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">10-K,</FONT> quarterly reports on Form <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">10-Q,</FONT> and current reports
on Form <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">8-K.</FONT> The Company will also be required to comply with all other obligations of the 1934 Act applicable to issuers filing registration statements pursuant to Section&nbsp;12(g) of the 1934 Act.
Additionally, the Company will be subject to the proxy rules in Section&nbsp;14 of the 1934 Act and the Company, trustees, officers, and principal shareholders will be subject to the reporting requirements of Sections 13 and 16 of the 1934 Act. The
SEC maintains a website at <U>www.sec.gov</U>, via which the Company&#8217;s SEC filings can be electronically accessed, including this Registration Statement and the exhibits and schedules hereto. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">After filing this Registration Statement, the Company will file an election to be regulated as a BDC under the 1940 Act as soon as reasonably
practicable. Upon filing such election, the Company will become subject to the 1940 Act requirements applicable to BDCs. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Investing in

outstanding Shares as of the end of any given quarter. </P></TD></TR></TABLE> <P STYLE="font-size:6pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>
<TABLE STYLE="BORDER-COLLAPSE:COLLAPSE; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt" BORDER="0" CELLPADDING="0" CELLSPACING="0" WIDTH="100%">
<TR style = "page-break-inside:avoid">
<TD WIDTH="5%">&nbsp;</TD>
<TD WIDTH="3%" VALIGN="top" ALIGN="left">&#149;</TD>
<TD WIDTH="1%" VALIGN="top">&nbsp;</TD>
<TD ALIGN="left" VALIGN="top"> <P ALIGN="left" STYLE=" margin-top:0pt ; margin-bottom:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt">The private companies and below investment grade securities in which the Company will invest may be difficult to
value and are generally illiquid. </P></TD></TR></TABLE> <P STYLE="font-size:6pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>
<TABLE STYLE="BORDER-COLLAPSE:COLLAPSE; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt" BORDER="0" CELLPADDING="0" CELLSPACING="0" WIDTH="100%">
<TR style = "page-break-inside:avoid">
<TD WIDTH="5%">&nbsp;</TD>
<TD WIDTH="3%" VALIGN="top" ALIGN="left">&#149;</TD>
<TD WIDTH="1%" VALIGN="top">&nbsp;</TD>
<TD ALIGN="left" VALIGN="top"> <P ALIGN="left" STYLE=" margin-top:0pt ; margin-bottom:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt">The Company intends to invest primarily in private companies for which very little public information exists.
Such companies are also generally more vulnerable to economic downturns and may experience substantial variations in operating results. </P></TD></TR></TABLE> <P STYLE="font-size:6pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>

<TD ALIGN="left" VALIGN="top"> <P ALIGN="left" STYLE=" margin-top:0pt ; margin-bottom:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt">Distributions may be funded from borrowings, which may constitute a return of capital and reduce the amount of
capital available to the Company for investment. Any capital returned to holders of Shares through distributions will be distributed after the payment of fees and expenses. </P></TD></TR></TABLE>

<TD ALIGN="left" VALIGN="top"> <P ALIGN="left" STYLE=" margin-top:0pt ; margin-bottom:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt">The Company may pay distributions in significant part from sources that may not be available in the future and
that are unrelated to the Company&#8217;s performance. This may reduce an investor&#8217;s adjusted tax basis in the Shares, thereby increasing the investor&#8217;s potential taxable gain or reducing the potential taxable loss on the sale of Shares.
</P></TD></TR></TABLE> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">As a result, there is a risk of a substantial loss on an investment in the Shares. See &#8220;<I>Item 1A. Risk
Factors</I>&#8221; for more information about these and other risks relating to the Shares. </P>

<h5 align="left" style="font-size:10pt;font-weight:bold"><a href="#toc">Table of Contents</a></h5>


<Center><DIV STYLE="width:8.5in" align="left">

<TABLE STYLE="BORDER-COLLAPSE:COLLAPSE; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt" BORDER="0" CELLPADDING="0" CELLSPACING="0" WIDTH="100%">
<TR style = "page-break-inside:avoid">
<TD WIDTH="10%" VALIGN="top" ALIGN="left"><B><A NAME="tx807896_4"></A>ITEM&#8201;1.</B></TD>
<TD ALIGN="left" VALIGN="top"> <P STYLE=" margin-top:0pt ; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman; " ALIGN="left"><B>BUSINESS </B></P></TD></TR></TABLE>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>Company&#8212;Adams Street Credit Solutions Fund </B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Company was formed on March&nbsp;29, 2019, as a Delaware limited liability company named Adams Street Private Credit BDC, LLC. On
January&nbsp;15, 2025, the Company converted to a Delaware limited partnership and was renamed Adams Street Credit Solutions Fund, LP. The Company is an externally managed, <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-diversified,</FONT> <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">closed-end</FONT> management investment company that intends to elect to be regulated as a BDC under the 1940 Act (the &#8220;<B>BDC Election</B>&#8221;). The Adviser, a Delaware limited liability company and subsidiary of
Adams Street, serves as the Company&#8217;s investment adviser and is responsible for portfolio and risk management of the Company. Subject to the overall supervision of the Board, the majority of whom are independent as required by the 1940 Act,
the Adviser will manage the Company&#8217;s <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">day-to-day</FONT></FONT> operations and provide investment advisory and management services to the Company. The Company also intends to
elect to be treated, and intends to qualify annually thereafter, as a RIC under Subchapter M of the Code, beginning with its tax year ending December&nbsp;31, 2026, or such later date as determined by the Company, for U.S. federal income tax
purposes. As a BDC and a RIC, the Company will be required to comply with certain regulatory requirements. See &#8220;<I>Item 1. Business &#8212; Regulation as a BDC</I>&#8221; and &#8220;<I>Item 1. Business &#8212; Certain U.S. Federal Income Tax
Considerations</I>.&#8221; The Company is the successor to Adams Street Credit Solutions Fund, LP, a Delaware limited partnership, and prior thereto, a Delaware limited liability company, that was exempt from registration under the 1940 Act pursuant
to Section&nbsp;3(c)(7) thereof (&#8220;<B>WLP</B>&#8221;). On August&nbsp;5, 2025, a reorganization of WLP into the Company was effected, under which WLP converted from a Delaware limited partnership to a Delaware statutory trust and the Company
was renamed Adams Street Credit Solutions Fund. The Company maintains an investment program and management team that are, in all material respects, equivalent to those of WLP. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Company&#8217;s investment objective is to generate current income and capital appreciation. The Company will seek to achieve its
investment objective primarily through investing in direct originations of Middle Market Senior Loans, including first lien senior secured loans (which may include stand-alone first lien loans, first lien/last out loans and &#8220;unitranche&#8221;
loans) and second lien senior secured loans, with the balance of its assets invested in higher yielding investments (which may include unsecured debt, mezzanine debt and investments in equities). The Middle Market Senior Loans are generally made to
private U.S. middle market companies that are, in many cases, controlled by private equity firms. As a BDC, the Company generally will be required to invest at least 70% of its assets in Qualifying Assets, but the Company may invest up to 30% of its
portfolio in <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-qualifying</FONT> assets, including companies domiciled in Europe and other countries outside of the United States, entities that are operating pursuant to certain exceptions under the 1940 Act and
publicly traded entities whose public equity market capitalization exceeds the levels provided for under the 1940 Act. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Company may
invest in cash, cash equivalents, U.S. government securities or high-quality debt securities maturing in one year or less from the time of investment, which are referred to herein, collectively, as temporary investments, so that 70% of the
Company&#8217;s assets would be Qualifying Assets. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Company&#8217;s investment strategy also includes a smaller allocation to more
liquid credit investments such as broadly syndicated loans and corporate bonds. The Company&#8217;s liquid credit instruments may include senior secured loans, senior secured bonds, high yield bonds and structured credit instruments (including
collateralized loan obligations (&#8220;<B>CLOs</B>&#8221;)). The Company intends to use these investments to maintain liquidity for its Share repurchase program and manage cash before investing subscription proceeds into originated loans, while
also seeking attractive investment returns. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Under normal circumstances, the Company will invest at least 80% of its net assets (plus the
amount of any borrowings for investment purposes) in credit-related instruments issued by corporate issuers (including loans, notes, bonds and other corporate debt securities). The Company&#8217;s 80% policy with respect to investments in
credit-related instruments is not fundamental and may be changed by the Board of Trustees without the approval of Shareholders. Shareholders will be provided with at least sixty (60)&nbsp;days&#8217; notice in the manner prescribed by the SEC before
making any change to this policy. </P>
 <p STYLE="margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt ; font-size:8pt">&nbsp;</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman" ALIGN="center">8 </P>

<Center><DIV STYLE="width:8.5in" align="left">
 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Company expects that most of its debt investments will be unrated. When rated by a
nationally recognized statistical ratings organization, the Company expects that its debt investments will generally carry a rating below investment grade (rated lower than &#8220;Baa3&#8221; by Moody&#8217;s Ratings or lower than <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">&#8220;BBB-&#8221;</FONT> by Standard&nbsp;&amp; Poor&#8217;s Rating Services), which is often referred to as &#8220;junk.&#8221; </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Company may, but is not required to, make investments in companies operating in workout or bankruptcy modes. Such investments present
additional legal risks, including fraudulent conveyance, voidable preference and equitable subordination risks. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Company may, but is
not required to, enter into interest rate, foreign exchange, and/or other derivative arrangements to hedge interest rate, currency, credit and/or other risks. While the Company primarily expects to invest in loans and securities denominated in U.S.
dollars, the Company may also invest in companies with operations outside of the United States, such as in Canada, the United Kingdom (the &#8220;<B>UK</B>&#8221;) and Europe, which may oblige the Company to invest in loans and/or securities
denominated in <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-U.S.</FONT> dollar currencies. In such event, the Company may enter into foreign exchange derivatives and forward transactions to mitigate the impact of movements in foreign exchange on the return
of such investments in U.S. dollar terms. These hedging activities, which will be subject to the applicable legal and regulatory compliance requirements, may include the use of futures, options and forward contracts. Any derivative agreements
entered into for speculative purposes are not expected to be material to the Company&#8217;s business or results of operations. The Company intends to operate and qualify as a &#8220;limited derivatives user&#8221; and has adopted compliance
policies to monitor the Company&#8217;s derivatives exposure in accordance with Rule <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">18f-4</FONT> under the 1940 Act (&#8220;<B>Rule <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">18f-4</FONT></B>&#8221;). The Company will bear
the costs incurred in connection with entering into, administering and settling any such derivative contracts. There can be no assurance any hedging strategy that the Company employs will be successful. See &#8220;<I>Item 1A. Risk
Factors&#8212;Limitations on Use of Derivatives</I>.&#8221; </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Company will employ leverage as market conditions permit and at the
discretion of the Adviser, but in no event will leverage employed exceed the limitations set forth in the 1940 Act. Pursuant to the 1940 Act, and as approved by the Board of Trustees and the Company&#8217;s initial Shareholder, the Company is
required to have an asset coverage of at least 150%, which means for every $100 of net assets the Company holds, the Company may raise $200 from borrowing and issuing senior securities (including debt and preferred shares). Any such leverage would
be expected to increase the total capital available for investment by the Company. The Company intends to use leverage in the form of: (i)&nbsp;the issuance of Series A Preferred Shares (as defined below), and may in the future issue additional
series of preferred shares, though it has no intention to do so; and (ii)&nbsp;a senior secured revolving credit facility with Wells Fargo Bank, National Association (&#8220;<B>Wells Fargo</B>&#8221;), the proceeds from which have been used to
facilitate the Company&#8217;s initial acquisitions of Middle Market Senior Loans and pay related expenses. In addition, Adams Street Partners, L.P. issued the Company an unsecured promissory note, the proceeds from which have been used to
facilitate certain acquisitions of Middle Market Senior Loans (the &#8220;<B>ASP Note</B>&#8221;); however, the Company intends to repay any amounts outstanding under the ASP Note in connection with the BDC Election. Following the BDC Election, the
Company may determine to <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">re-draw</FONT> amounts under, or alternatively terminate, the ASP Note. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">To
achieve its investment objective, the Company will leverage the experience, talent and extensive network of relationships of Adams Street, its personnel, and Adams Street&#8217;s dedicated private credit investment team (the &#8220;<B>Private Credit
Team</B>&#8221;) to source and evaluate opportunities. There are no assurances that the Company will achieve its investment objective. The Company&#8217;s administrative and executive offices are located at One North Wacker Drive, Suite 2700,
Chicago, IL 60606. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>Formation Transactions </B></P>

on January&nbsp;15, 2025. The Company is the successor to WLP, a Delaware limited partnership that was exempt from registration under the 1940 Act pursuant to Section&nbsp;3(c)(7) thereof. On </P>

Registered &#8212; Preferred Shares.</I>&#8221; </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:24pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>Adams Street Firm History </B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Adams Street is a leading private markets investment firm, providing private credit, private equity primary and secondary partnership
investments, <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">co-investment,</FONT> and direct growth equity investment management capabilities to institutional investors. Adams Street will provide investment advisory services to pooled investment vehicles,
including the Company, other business development companies and commingled private funds, separately managed accounts, funds of one and other similar vehicles and accounts (each, an &#8220;<B>ASP Entity</B>&#8221;). Adams Street is one of the oldest
and largest private markets investment managers in the world. Together with its predecessor organizations, Adams Street has been managing direct growth equity investments since 1972. Adams Street established the first private equity fund of funds
for institutional investors in 1979 and has been a pioneer in the development of the secondary market, completing its first secondary investment in 1986. As a significant, long-term investor in private markets, Adams Street has a meaningful
information advantage that benefits each strategy. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Adams Street is well-known globally for its continuous commitment to, and deep
understanding of, the private markets industry. As of December&nbsp;31, 2025, the firm had approximately $65&nbsp;billion of assets under management, 15 offices in 11 countries, and investments spanning more than 30 countries. Adams Street believes
a global outlook combined with deep local knowledge is the key to long-term, sustainable investment success. </P>

<Center><DIV STYLE="width:8.5in" align="left">
 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Adams Street&#8217;s legacy began at First National Bank of Chicago (&#8220;<B>First
Chicago</B>&#8221;) in 1972. In 1989, Adams Street&#8217;s predecessor organization, Brinson Partners, Inc., was organized and acquired the institutional asset management business from First Chicago. In 1995, Brinson Partners, Inc. and Swiss Bank
Corporation (&#8220;<B>SBC</B>&#8221;) combined their international institutional investment management organizations into a single investment management business. Union Bank of Switzerland and SBC subsequently merged in June 1998 to form UBS AG.
Adams Street spun out of UBS AG on January&nbsp;1, 2001 and was composed of the members of Brinson Partners&#8217; Private Equity Group. Today, Adams Street is an independent, 100% employee-owned organization. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">By combining all of these investment strategies into a single, global integrated platform, Adams Street aims to capitalize on knowledge, data,
insights, and relationships that are not available to firms pursuing any one strategy. While each investing partner at Adams Street is primarily focused on their core strategy, there is shared compensation and knowledge at the firm level, which
Adams Street believes reinforces a culture built around collaboration, teamwork, and partnership. In Adams Street&#8217;s view, this synergy is the foundation for Adams Street&#8217;s long history of success and a key competitive advantage. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>Adviser </B></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Adviser, a Delaware limited
liability company, is a wholly-owned subsidiary of Adams Street, and Adams Street serves as the sole member of the Adviser. The Adviser is registered with the SEC under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, as amended (the &#8220;<B>Advisers
Act</B>&#8221;). The Adviser&#8217;s principal place of business is in Chicago, Illinois. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Adviser serves as the Company&#8217;s
investment adviser pursuant to an investment advisory agreement with the Company dated August&nbsp;19, 2025 (the &#8220;<B>Investment Advisory Agreement</B>&#8221;). Subject to the overall supervision of the Board, the Adviser is responsible for
managing the Company&#8217;s business affairs, including sourcing investment opportunities, performing research and due diligence, structuring investments and monitoring the Company&#8217;s portfolio on an ongoing basis through the Private Credit
Team. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Adviser will seek to leverage the extensive network and deep experience of the Private Credit Team to prioritize what it
believes to be the most compelling investment opportunities for the Company. All investment decisions will require the approval of the Private Credit Team&#8217;s investment committee (the &#8220;<B>Investment Committee</B>&#8221;). </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Adviser and its affiliates may provide management or investment services to others whose objectives overlap with the Company&#8217;s. The
Adviser may face conflicts in the allocation of investment opportunities to the Company and other ASP Entities. To address these conflicts, the Adviser has put in place an investment allocation policy that seeks to ensure fair and equitable
allocation of investment opportunities over time and address the <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">co-investment</FONT> restrictions set forth under the 1940 Act (the &#8220;<B>Allocation Policy</B>&#8221;). See &#8220;<I>Item&nbsp;1A. Risk
Factors&#8212;Certain Conflicts of Interest&#8212;Work on Other Projects; Allocation of Personnel</I>&#8221; and &#8220;<I>Allocation of Investment Opportunities</I>.&#8221; </P>

capacity as the Administrator, provides, or oversees the performance of, certain administrative and compliance services. The Company is obligated to reimburse the Administrator and/or its affiliates for its costs, expenses and the Company&#8217;s

 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Administrator, on behalf of the Company and at the Company&#8217;s expense, may retain

<P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>Board of Trustees </B></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Overall responsibility
for the Company&#8217;s oversight rests with the Board of Trustees. The Company has entered into the Investment Advisory Agreement with the Adviser, pursuant to which the Adviser will manage the Company on a <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">day-to-day</FONT></FONT> basis as described herein. The Board of Trustees is responsible for overseeing the Adviser and other service providers in the Company&#8217;s operations in accordance with the provisions of the
1940 Act, the Company&#8217;s Amended and Restated Declaration of Trust (the &#8220;<B>Declaration of Trust</B>&#8221;) and <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">By-Laws</FONT> (&#8220;<B><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">By-Laws</FONT></B>&#8221; and
together with the Declaration of Trust, the &#8220;<B>Organizational Documents</B>&#8221;) and applicable provisions of state and other laws. The Adviser will keep the Board of Trustees well informed as to the Adviser&#8217;s activities on the

(5)&nbsp;trustees (the &#8220;<B>Trustees</B>&#8221; and each, a &#8220;<B>Trustee</B>&#8221;), three (3)&nbsp;of whom are Trustees who are not &#8220;interested persons&#8221; (as that term is defined in the 1940 Act) of the Company or the Adviser
(the &#8220;<B>Independent Trustees</B>&#8221;). The Board of Trustees meets at regularly scheduled quarterly meetings each year. In addition, the Board of Trustees may hold special in- person or telephonic meetings or informal conference calls to
discuss specific matters that may arise or require action between regular meetings and may also act by unanimous consent. As described below, the Board of Trustees has established an audit committee (the &#8220;<B>Audit Committee</B>&#8221;) and a
nominating and governance committee (the &#8220;<B>Nominating and Governance Committee</B>&#8221;), and may establish ad hoc committees or working groups from time to time, to assist the Board of Trustees in fulfilling its oversight
responsibilities. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>Market Opportunity </B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Adams Street believes that increasing regulation has caused U.S. commercial banks to substantially reduce their lending to middle-market
companies. At the same time, demand for debt capital, particularly in the market for private equity-backed leveraged buyouts, has continued to grow. It is Adams Street&#8217;s belief that this demand/supply imbalance has helped make the yields and
terms that can be obtained from the private debt issued by middle-market companies comparatively more attractive than many other investment alternatives available in the credit markets today.</P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">As compared to broadly syndicated loans and public high yield bonds, private middle-market debt has a number of advantages:</P>
<P STYLE="font-size:6pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>
<TABLE STYLE="BORDER-COLLAPSE:COLLAPSE; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt" BORDER="0" CELLPADDING="0" CELLSPACING="0" WIDTH="100%">
<TR style = "page-break-inside:avoid">
<TD WIDTH="5%">&nbsp;</TD>
<TD WIDTH="3%" VALIGN="top" ALIGN="left">&#149;</TD>
<TD WIDTH="1%" VALIGN="top">&nbsp;</TD>
<TD ALIGN="left" VALIGN="top"> <P ALIGN="left" STYLE=" margin-top:0pt ; margin-bottom:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt">It has historically priced at a premium.</P></TD></TR></TABLE>
<P STYLE="font-size:6pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>
<TABLE STYLE="BORDER-COLLAPSE:COLLAPSE; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt" BORDER="0" CELLPADDING="0" CELLSPACING="0" WIDTH="100%">
<TR style = "page-break-inside:avoid">
<TD WIDTH="5%">&nbsp;</TD>
<TD WIDTH="3%" VALIGN="top" ALIGN="left">&#149;</TD>
<TD WIDTH="1%" VALIGN="top">&nbsp;</TD>
<TD ALIGN="left" VALIGN="top"> <P ALIGN="left" STYLE=" margin-top:0pt ; margin-bottom:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt">It is usually a component of more conservative capital structures that are less leveraged.</P></TD></TR></TABLE>
<P STYLE="font-size:6pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>
<TABLE STYLE="BORDER-COLLAPSE:COLLAPSE; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt" BORDER="0" CELLPADDING="0" CELLSPACING="0" WIDTH="100%">
<TR style = "page-break-inside:avoid">
<TD WIDTH="5%">&nbsp;</TD>
<TD WIDTH="3%" VALIGN="top" ALIGN="left">&#149;</TD>
<TD WIDTH="1%" VALIGN="top">&nbsp;</TD>
<TD ALIGN="left" VALIGN="top"> <P ALIGN="left" STYLE=" margin-top:0pt ; margin-bottom:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt">It typically contains more robust covenants and lender-friendly protections.</P></TD></TR></TABLE>
<P STYLE="font-size:6pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>
<TABLE STYLE="BORDER-COLLAPSE:COLLAPSE; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt" BORDER="0" CELLPADDING="0" CELLSPACING="0" WIDTH="100%">
<TR style = "page-break-inside:avoid">
<TD WIDTH="5%">&nbsp;</TD>
<TD WIDTH="3%" VALIGN="top" ALIGN="left">&#149;</TD>
<TD WIDTH="1%" VALIGN="top">&nbsp;</TD>
<TD ALIGN="left" VALIGN="top"> <P ALIGN="left" STYLE=" margin-top:0pt ; margin-bottom:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt">It has experienced lower default rates and higher recoveries. </P></TD></TR></TABLE>
<P STYLE="font-size:6pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>
<TABLE STYLE="BORDER-COLLAPSE:COLLAPSE; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt" BORDER="0" CELLPADDING="0" CELLSPACING="0" WIDTH="100%">
<TR style = "page-break-inside:avoid">
<TD WIDTH="5%">&nbsp;</TD>
<TD WIDTH="3%" VALIGN="top" ALIGN="left">&#149;</TD>
<TD WIDTH="1%" VALIGN="top">&nbsp;</TD>
<TD ALIGN="left" VALIGN="top"> <P ALIGN="left" STYLE=" margin-top:0pt ; margin-bottom:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt">As compared to high-yield bonds, it provides exposure to floating-rate debt, which is less sensitive to interest
rate changes from a <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">mark-to-market</FONT></FONT> perspective. </P></TD></TR></TABLE>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">In the past, commercial banks were a primary source of capital for middle-market companies. Towards the end of the 1990s, the banks began to
substantially reduce the leveraged loans they were willing to hold. This reduction was accomplished, in large part, by syndicating the unwanted exposure into the institutional loan </P>
 <p STYLE="margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt ; font-size:8pt">&nbsp;</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman" ALIGN="center">12 </P>

</DIV></Center>


<p style="margin-top:1em; margin-bottom:0em; page-break-before:always"> </p>
<HR SIZE="3" style="COLOR:#999999" WIDTH="100%" ALIGN="CENTER">
<h5 align="left" style="font-size:10pt;font-weight:bold"><a href="#toc">Table of Contents</a></h5>


<Center><DIV STYLE="width:8.5in" align="left">
 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">
market. Because most buyers of loans in the institutional market required liquidity, smaller, less liquid middle-market loans that were not as easily syndicated or traded, were <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">de-emphasized</FONT> by the banks. In addition, regulations such as the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act (&#8220;<B>Dodd-Frank</B>&#8221;) and the Third Basel Accord (Basel III) further restrained
commercial banks&#8217; ability to lend money.</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">While, as a result of the banks&#8217; withdrawal, debt capital was becoming scarce, demand
was continuing to grow. The growing demand was fueled, to a significant extent, by private equity sponsors, who raised substantial pools of capital and needed the debt to help finance their buyouts.</P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">In recent years, private credit has further taken share from the broadly syndicated loan market because it has been a more stable and flexible
source of financing for private equity firms.</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Adams Street believes that the combination of premium pricing and better performance with
respect to defaults and recoveries makes private debt a compelling investment proposition. In Adams Street&#8217;s opinion, the factors that helped create these favorable conditions in the market for private debt are both structural and secular in
nature and therefore are likely to be long lasting. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:24pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>Investment Strategy </B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Company&#8217;s investment objective is to generate current income and capital appreciation. The Company will seek to achieve its
investment objective primarily through investing in direct originations of Middle Market Senior Loans, including first lien senior secured loans (which may include stand-alone first lien loans, first lien/last out loans and &#8220;unitranche&#8221;
loans) and second lien senior secured loans, with the balance of its assets invested in higher yielding investments (which may include unsecured debt, mezzanine debt and investments in equities). The Middle Market Senior Loans are generally made to
private U.S. middle market companies that are, in many cases, controlled by private equity firms. As a BDC, the Company generally will be required to invest at least 70% of its assets in Qualifying Assets, but the Company may invest up to 30% of its
portfolio in non-qualifying assets, including companies domiciled in Europe and other countries outside of the United States, entities that are operating pursuant to certain exceptions under the 1940 Act and publicly traded entities whose public
equity market capitalization exceeds the levels provided for under the 1940 Act. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Company may invest in cash, cash equivalents, U.S.
government securities or high-quality debt securities maturing in one year or less from the time of investment, which are referred to herein, collectively, as temporary investments, so that 70% of the Company&#8217;s assets would be Qualifying
Assets. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Company&#8217;s investment strategy also includes a smaller allocation to more liquid credit investments such as broadly
syndicated loans and corporate bonds. The Company&#8217;s liquid credit instruments may include senior secured loans, senior secured bonds, high yield bonds and structured credit instruments (including CLOs). The Company intends to use these
investments to maintain liquidity for its Share repurchase program and manage cash before investing subscription proceeds into originated loans, while also seeking attractive investment returns. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Under normal circumstances, the Company will invest at least 80% of its net assets (plus the amount of any borrowings for investment purposes)
in credit-related instruments issued by corporate issuers (including loans, notes, bonds and other corporate debt securities). The Company&#8217;s 80% policy with respect to investments in credit-related instruments is not fundamental and may be
changed by the Board of Trustees without Shareholder approval. Shareholders will be provided with at least sixty (60)&nbsp;days&#8217; notice in the manner prescribed by the SEC before making any change to this policy. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Most of the Company&#8217;s debt investments are expected to be unrated. When rated by a nationally recognized statistical ratings
organization, the Company expects that its debt investments will generally carry a rating below </P>
 <p STYLE="margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt ; font-size:8pt">&nbsp;</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman" ALIGN="center">13 </P>

</DIV></Center>


<p style="margin-top:1em; margin-bottom:0em; page-break-before:always"> </p>
<HR SIZE="3" style="COLOR:#999999" WIDTH="100%" ALIGN="CENTER">
<h5 align="left" style="font-size:10pt;font-weight:bold"><a href="#toc">Table of Contents</a></h5>


<Center><DIV STYLE="width:8.5in" align="left">
 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">
investment grade (rated lower than &#8220;Baa3&#8221; by Moody&#8217;s Ratings or lower than <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">&#8220;BBB-&#8221;</FONT> by Standard&nbsp;&amp; Poor&#8217;s Rating
Services), which is often referred to as &#8220;junk.&#8221; </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Company may, but is not required to, make investments in companies
operating in workout or bankruptcy modes. Such investments present additional legal risks, including fraudulent conveyance, voidable preference and equitable subordination risks. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Company may, but is not required to, enter into interest rate, foreign exchange, and/or other derivative arrangements to hedge interest
rate, currency, credit and/or other risks. While the Company primarily expects to invest in loans and securities denominated in U.S. dollars, the Company may also invest in companies with operations outside of the United States, such as in Canada,
the UK and Europe, which may oblige the Company to invest in loans and/or securities denominated in <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-U.S.</FONT> dollar currencies. In such event, the Company may enter into foreign exchange derivatives and
forward transactions to mitigate the impact of movements in foreign exchange on the return of such investments in U.S. dollar terms. These hedging activities, which will be subject to the applicable legal and regulatory compliance requirements, may
include the use of futures, options and forward contracts. Any derivative agreements entered into for speculative purposes are not expected to be material to the Company&#8217;s business or results of operations. The Company intends to operate and
qualify as a &#8220;limited derivatives user&#8221; and has adopted compliance policies to monitor the Company&#8217;s derivatives exposure in accordance with Rule <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">18f-4.</FONT> The Company will bear the costs
incurred in connection with entering into, administering and settling any such derivative contracts. There can be no assurance any hedging strategy that the Company employs will be successful. See &#8220;<I>Item 1A. Risk Factors &#8212; Limitations
on Use of Derivatives</I>.&#8221; </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Company will employ leverage as market conditions permit and at the discretion of the Adviser, but
in no event will leverage employed exceed the limitations set forth in the 1940 Act. Pursuant to the 1940 Act, and as approved by the Board of Trustees and the Company&#8217;s initial Shareholder, the Company is required to have an asset coverage of
at least 150%, which means for every $100 of net assets the Company holds, the Company may raise $200 from borrowing and issuing senior securities (including debt and preferred shares). Any such leverage, if incurred, would be expected to increase
the total capital available for investment by the Company. The Company intends to use leverage in the form of the issuance of the Series A Preferred Shares, and may in the future issue additional series of preferred shares, though it has no
intention to do so. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>Structure of Investments </B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Debt Investments. </I></B>The terms of the Company&#8217;s debt investments will be tailored to the facts and circumstances of each
transaction. The Adviser will seek to negotiate the structure of each investment to protect the Company&#8217;s rights and manage its risks. The Company intends to invest in the following types of debt: </P>
<P STYLE="font-size:6pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>
<TABLE STYLE="BORDER-COLLAPSE:COLLAPSE; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt" BORDER="0" CELLPADDING="0" CELLSPACING="0" WIDTH="100%">

<TD ALIGN="left" VALIGN="top"> <P ALIGN="left" STYLE=" margin-top:0pt ; margin-bottom:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt"><I>First lien debt. </I>First lien debt is typically senior on a lien basis to other liabilities in the
issuer&#8217;s capital structure and has the benefit of a first priority security interest in assets of the issuer. The security interest ranks above the security interest of any second lien lenders in those assets. The Company&#8217;s first lien
debt may include stand-alone first lien loans, &#8220;unitranche&#8221; loans and first lien secured bonds. </P></TD></TR></TABLE> <P STYLE="font-size:6pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>
<TABLE STYLE="BORDER-COLLAPSE:COLLAPSE; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt" BORDER="0" CELLPADDING="0" CELLSPACING="0" WIDTH="100%">

<TD WIDTH="10%">&nbsp;</TD>
<TD WIDTH="2%" VALIGN="top" ALIGN="left">&#149;</TD>
<TD WIDTH="1%" VALIGN="top">&nbsp;</TD>
<TD ALIGN="left" VALIGN="top"> <P ALIGN="left" STYLE=" margin-top:0pt ; margin-bottom:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt"><I>Stand-alone first lien loans. </I>Stand-alone first lien loans are traditional first lien loans. All lenders
in the facility have equal rights to the collateral that is subject to the first priority security interest. </P></TD></TR></TABLE> <P STYLE="font-size:6pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>
<TABLE STYLE="BORDER-COLLAPSE:COLLAPSE; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt" BORDER="0" CELLPADDING="0" CELLSPACING="0" WIDTH="100%">
<TR style = "page-break-inside:avoid">
<TD WIDTH="10%">&nbsp;</TD>
<TD WIDTH="2%" VALIGN="top" ALIGN="left">&#149;</TD>
<TD WIDTH="1%" VALIGN="top">&nbsp;</TD>
<TD ALIGN="left" VALIGN="top"> <P ALIGN="left" STYLE=" margin-top:0pt ; margin-bottom:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt">&#8220;<I>Unitranche&#8221; loans</I>. Unitranche loans are loans that combine both senior and subordinated debt,
generally in a first lien position. In many cases, &#8220;unitranche&#8221; lenders, may provide the issuer most, if not all, of the capital structure above the equity. </P></TD></TR></TABLE>
<P STYLE="font-size:6pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>
<TABLE STYLE="BORDER-COLLAPSE:COLLAPSE; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt" BORDER="0" CELLPADDING="0" CELLSPACING="0" WIDTH="100%">
<TR style = "page-break-inside:avoid">
<TD WIDTH="10%">&nbsp;</TD>
<TD WIDTH="2%" VALIGN="top" ALIGN="left">&#149;</TD>
<TD WIDTH="1%" VALIGN="top">&nbsp;</TD>
<TD ALIGN="left" VALIGN="top"> <P ALIGN="left" STYLE=" margin-top:0pt ; margin-bottom:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt"><I>First lien secured bonds</I>. First lien secured bonds are similar to stand-alone first lien loans. All
investors in the bond have equal rights to the collateral that is subject to the first priority security interest. </P></TD></TR></TABLE> <P STYLE="font-size:6pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>
<TABLE STYLE="BORDER-COLLAPSE:COLLAPSE; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt" BORDER="0" CELLPADDING="0" CELLSPACING="0" WIDTH="100%">
<TR style = "page-break-inside:avoid">
<TD WIDTH="5%">&nbsp;</TD>

<TD ALIGN="left" VALIGN="top"> <P ALIGN="left" STYLE=" margin-top:0pt ; margin-bottom:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt"><I>Second lien debt. </I>Second lien debt may include second lien secured loans, and, to a lesser extent, second
lien secured bonds, with a secondary priority behind first lien debt. Second lien debt typically is </P></TD></TR></TABLE>
 <p STYLE="margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt ; font-size:8pt">&nbsp;</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman" ALIGN="center">14 </P>

senior on a lien basis to other liabilities in the issuer&#8217;s capital structure and has the benefit of a security interest over assets of the issuer, though ranking junior to first lien debt
secured by those assets. </P></TD></TR></TABLE> <P STYLE="font-size:6pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>
<TABLE STYLE="BORDER-COLLAPSE:COLLAPSE; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt" BORDER="0" CELLPADDING="0" CELLSPACING="0" WIDTH="100%">

<TD ALIGN="left" VALIGN="top"> <P ALIGN="left" STYLE=" margin-top:0pt ; margin-bottom:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt"><I>Unsecured debt. </I>Unsecured debt usually ranks subordinate in priority of payment to first lien and second
lien debt and may not have the benefit of financial covenants common in first lien and second lien debt. However, unsecured debt ranks senior to common and preferred equity in an issuer&#8217;s capital structure. Unsecured debt generally offers
fixed returns in the form of interest payments. Due to its higher risk profile and often less restrictive covenants compared to first lien and second lien debt, unsecured debt generally bears a higher stated interest rate than first lien and second
lien debt. </P></TD></TR></TABLE> <P STYLE="font-size:6pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>
<TABLE STYLE="BORDER-COLLAPSE:COLLAPSE; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt" BORDER="0" CELLPADDING="0" CELLSPACING="0" WIDTH="100%">

<TD ALIGN="left" VALIGN="top"> <P ALIGN="left" STYLE=" margin-top:0pt ; margin-bottom:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt"><I>Securitized debt</I>. The Company&#8217;s CLO investments will be backed by a portfolio of senior secured
loans and may include senior or mezzanine CLO debt tranches (rated investment grade), mezzanine CLO debt tranches (rated below investment grade or unrated), subordinated CLO equity tranches (unrated), leveraged loans (including third-party-managed
warehouse facilities that hold such loans in anticipation of expected CLO issuance) and vehicles that invest indirectly in CLO securities or leveraged loans. </P></TD></TR></TABLE>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Company&#8217;s debt investments will typically be structured with the maximum seniority and collateral that the Company can reasonably
obtain while seeking to achieve its total return target. The Adviser will seek to limit the downside potential of the Company&#8217;s investments by: </P> <P STYLE="font-size:6pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>
<TABLE STYLE="BORDER-COLLAPSE:COLLAPSE; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt" BORDER="0" CELLPADDING="0" CELLSPACING="0" WIDTH="100%">

<TD ALIGN="left" VALIGN="top"> <P ALIGN="left" STYLE=" margin-top:0pt ; margin-bottom:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt">mitigating <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">non-credit</FONT> related risks on the Company&#8217;s investments,
including call protection provisions to protect future payment income. In addition, most of the Company&#8217;s investments are expected to be floating rate in nature, which the Adviser believes will help act as a portfolio-wide hedge against
inflation; and </P></TD></TR></TABLE> <P STYLE="font-size:6pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>
<TABLE STYLE="BORDER-COLLAPSE:COLLAPSE; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt" BORDER="0" CELLPADDING="0" CELLSPACING="0" WIDTH="100%">

<TD ALIGN="left" VALIGN="top"> <P ALIGN="left" STYLE=" margin-top:0pt ; margin-bottom:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt">negotiating covenants in connection with the Company&#8217;s investments consistent with preservation of the
Company&#8217;s capital. Such restrictions may include affirmative covenants (including reporting requirements), negative covenants (including financial covenants), lien protection, change of control provisions and, depending on the size, nature and
performance of the transaction, the Company may occupy a seat or serve as an observer on a portfolio company&#8217;s board of directors or similar governing body. </P></TD></TR></TABLE>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Within the Company&#8217;s portfolio, the Adviser will aim to maintain the appropriate proportion among the various types of first lien debt,
second lien debt and unsecured debt to allow the Company to achieve its investment objective while seeking to minimize the risk of permanent loss. There can be no assurance that the Company&#8217;s sought after investment characteristics will be
attained in any or all circumstances or that any strategy to limit downside risk will be successful. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Opportunistic
Investments.</I></B> Although not expected to be a primary component of the Company&#8217;s investment strategy, the Company may also selectively make investments in portfolios of loans, receivables or other debt instruments, traded loans and
securities of corporate issuers when market conditions create opportunities with a compelling risk profile, and potential strategic opportunities, including acquisitions of other private and public finance companies, business development companies
and asset managers. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Equity Investments.</I></B> In certain instances, the Company may also make equity or equity-related
investments (including common stock, preferred shares, securities convertible into common stock and warrants). </P>
 <p STYLE="margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt ; font-size:8pt">&nbsp;</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman" ALIGN="center">15 </P>

</DIV></Center>


<p style="margin-top:1em; margin-bottom:0em; page-break-before:always"> </p>

<h5 align="left" style="font-size:10pt;font-weight:bold"><a href="#toc">Table of Contents</a></h5>


<Center><DIV STYLE="width:8.5in" align="left">
 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>Investment Process </B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Sourcing </I></B></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Private Credit
Team&#8217;s investment process begins with sourcing investment opportunities, and the Company believes Adams Street&#8217;s core focus on private equity general partners and its integrated platform provide a highly differentiated sourcing advantage
and access to a large number of high-quality debt investment opportunities. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">A majority of opportunities are expected to come directly
from private equity sponsors already known to Adams Street either through: </P> <P STYLE="font-size:6pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>
<TABLE STYLE="BORDER-COLLAPSE:COLLAPSE; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt" BORDER="0" CELLPADDING="0" CELLSPACING="0" WIDTH="100%">
<TR style = "page-break-inside:avoid">
<TD WIDTH="5%">&nbsp;</TD>
<TD WIDTH="3%" VALIGN="top" ALIGN="left">&#149;</TD>
<TD WIDTH="1%" VALIGN="top">&nbsp;</TD>
<TD ALIGN="left" VALIGN="top"> <P ALIGN="left" STYLE=" margin-top:0pt ; margin-bottom:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt">Historical relationships originating from Adams Street&#8217;s existing primary investment, secondary investment,
or <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">co-investment</FONT> activities, or </P></TD></TR></TABLE> <P STYLE="font-size:6pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>
<TABLE STYLE="BORDER-COLLAPSE:COLLAPSE; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt" BORDER="0" CELLPADDING="0" CELLSPACING="0" WIDTH="100%">
<TR style = "page-break-inside:avoid">
<TD WIDTH="5%">&nbsp;</TD>
<TD WIDTH="3%" VALIGN="top" ALIGN="left">&#149;</TD>
<TD WIDTH="1%" VALIGN="top">&nbsp;</TD>
<TD ALIGN="left" VALIGN="top"> <P ALIGN="left" STYLE=" margin-top:0pt ; margin-bottom:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt">The Private Credit Team&#8217;s prior experience and existing individual relationships. </P></TD></TR></TABLE>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The longevity of Adams Street&#8217;s private equity investment program in primaries and secondaries, plus the breadth of its advisory board
seats, provides Adams Street with a distinct knowledge advantage and a preferred position in sourcing deals. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Adams Street has invested
with hundreds of private equity general partners (&#8220;<B>GPs</B>&#8221;) and currently holds hundreds of advisory board seats. Adams Street believes that these sponsor relationships, spanning across debt, equity, and strategic partnerships,
position the Company as a true financing partner as opposed to solely a source of debt financing. The Company is intended to benefit from Adams Street&#8217;s significant alignment with the sponsor community in several meaningful ways, including
(i)&nbsp;increased deal funnel as sponsor relationships across the firm drive new inbound financing opportunities, (ii)&nbsp;proprietary insight into sponsor portfolio companies, including financing structures and maturity information, which the
team can use to preempt refinancing conversations, (iii)&nbsp;opportunities to match competitor proposals (i.e., last look) and (iv)&nbsp;increased opportunities to obtain sole-sourced or leadership positions in investments, which often include
additional economics to the Company and greater control and oversight of the investment. In many instances, the Private Credit Team will have proprietary access to historical company information through Adams Street&#8217;s firmwide proprietary
database, which houses historical limited partner reporting packages, advisory board materials, and due diligence documents across active, prior, and potential GP relationships spanning 45+ years. These resources provide performance, strategy, and
valuation insights, which are often unavailable to Adams Street&#8217;s competitors and which provide the Company with a significant information advantage in the market. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The middle-market space in particular tends to be very relationship-oriented and, unlike the broadly syndicated market, a majority of debt
financing opportunities here are initiated directly by private equity sponsors. <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">Mid-market</FONT> opportunities, which comprise Adams Street&#8217;s main focus, are in fact not easily accessible to unknown third
parties. The fact that Adams Street has a deep and extensive network of relationships with private equity sponsors not only provides preferred access to opportunities, but also ensures Adams Street&#8217;s investment professionals are competitively
positioned to win deals. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">An additional source of deal flow is through investment banks, debt placement agents, attorneys, and
accountants. While Adams Street&#8217;s position in the market generates a good volume of inbound deal flow, active marketing (i.e., routine visits, telephone calls, and email correspondence with equity sponsors) by the Private Credit Team and Adams
Street as a whole is important to maintaining a steady flow of deals. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Screening&nbsp;&amp; Due Diligence </I></B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Private Credit Team&#8217;s interaction with the lead sponsor in connection with each investment is very important. Quick and thoughtful
feedback, efficient yet <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">in-depth</FONT> due diligence, and extensive third-party review (accounting, legal, etc.) are essential ingredients to maintaining a steady and productive flow of debt financing opportunities
over time. </P>
 <p STYLE="margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt ; font-size:8pt">&nbsp;</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman" ALIGN="center">16 </P>

</DIV></Center>


<p style="margin-top:1em; margin-bottom:0em; page-break-before:always"> </p>
<HR SIZE="3" style="COLOR:#999999" WIDTH="100%" ALIGN="CENTER">
<h5 align="left" style="font-size:10pt;font-weight:bold"><a href="#toc">Table of Contents</a></h5>


<Center><DIV STYLE="width:8.5in" align="left">
 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">After receiving information about a potential investment opportunity, the Private Credit
Team will quickly triage a deal and determine whether or not it merits further attention. Often, deals are declined during the screening process if the Private Credit Team determines that the prospective portfolio company or industry falls outside
of its investment parameters. To the extent the deal passes the initial screening, it then moves on to the diligence phase. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The diligence
effort is led by the Private Credit Team, in collaboration with the lead sponsor. This effort incorporates the sponsor&#8217;s due diligence on the prospective portfolio company investment, but goes further to include additional reference calls,
financial review, cash flow modeling/sensitivity analysis, meetings with management, site visits, industry diligence, and accounting and legal review. Due diligence progress is reported and discussed among the entire Private Credit Team as part of
their weekly team meetings, and in some cases more frequently. All members of the Private Credit Team are encouraged to participate in these deal discussions and provide feedback as to their assessment of prospective portfolio company risks and
opportunities. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Private Credit Team uses both internal and external research to support the broader investment and due diligence
process. Most investments start with a significant amount of desktop research, which leverages information that might already exist in Adams Street&#8217;s proprietary database and analytics tool, ASPIRE (Adams Street Partners Investment Research
Explorer), public filings, materials from previous transactions, etc. In addition, the Private Credit Team uses third-party data providers such as Preqin, CapIQ, LCD, and PitchBook to supplement internal and publicly available information resources.
The Private Credit Team also has access to equity research from investment banks, including all major bulge bracket banks. All of this ensures Adams Street&#8217;s investment teams have access to a broad range of industry data that enables them to
make more informed investment decisions. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Further, the Private Credit Team&#8217;s deep sponsor network provides industry and prospective
portfolio company specific research that is valuable and used during the investment process. In many instances, the Private Credit Team will have proprietary access to historical prospective portfolio company information through Adams Street&#8217;s
firmwide proprietary database, advisory board materials, and due diligence documents across active, prior, and potential GP relationships spanning 45+ years. These resources often provide performance, strategy and valuation insights, which are not
available to Adams Street&#8217;s competitors. Third-party research sources are also used to gain access to industry experts and are a critical, primary source of research used to evaluate potential investments. All of Adams Street&#8217;s research
as it relates to private credit is done by the Private Credit Team with help from Adams Street&#8217;s Performance Reporting and Analysis Team and Investment Strategy and Risk Management Team. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">While deal teams are responsible for driving the due diligence process, the Investment Committee is responsible for voting on proposed
investments. The Investment Committee meets regularly to discuss any potential investments. Adams Street&#8217;s investment process is built around a team-oriented decision-making function which leverages the collective experience of all members of
the investment team. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><I>Investment Criteria </I></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">In evaluating investment opportunities, Adams Street seeks to identify and invest in established issuers with a long history of profitability,
sustainable presence in their respective markets, backing by strong sponsors and led by experienced management teams. Some of the factors examined when making investment selections include: </P>
<P STYLE="font-size:6pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>

<TD ALIGN="left" VALIGN="top"> <P ALIGN="left" STYLE=" margin-top:0pt ; margin-bottom:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt">The experience, track record, and motivation of the lead sponsor; </P></TD></TR></TABLE>
<P STYLE="font-size:6pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>

of reinvestment; </P></TD></TR></TABLE> <P STYLE="font-size:6pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>

capital intensity, margin trends, variability of revenues, growth rates, etc.); </P></TD></TR></TABLE>

<TD ALIGN="left" VALIGN="top"> <P ALIGN="left" STYLE=" margin-top:0pt ; margin-bottom:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt">Capital structure considerations, including debt multiples, cost of capital, covenant levels, creditor
rights/protections, and level of equity contribution. </P></TD></TR></TABLE> <P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Monitoring </I></B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Adviser will employ an approach with respect to its investments whereby members of the Private Credit Team that are responsible for leading
and underwriting an investment are also responsible for its ongoing monitoring and risk management. The Adviser believes that this approach will lead to greater connectivity between the Adviser and its portfolio companies, improved access to
information and increased accountability, while simultaneously reducing the risk of knowledge loss that exists when the sourcing, due diligence and monitoring roles are bifurcated. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">After the investment decision is made and the deal is closed, the Private Credit Team remains responsible for proactively monitoring the
investment. The ongoing monitoring of investments conducted by the Private Credit Team includes: </P> <P STYLE="font-size:6pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>
<TABLE STYLE="BORDER-COLLAPSE:COLLAPSE; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt" BORDER="0" CELLPADDING="0" CELLSPACING="0" WIDTH="100%">

<TD ALIGN="left" VALIGN="top"> <P ALIGN="left" STYLE=" margin-top:0pt ; margin-bottom:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt">Portfolio company board observer seats (in certain cases) </P></TD></TR></TABLE>
<P STYLE="font-size:6pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>

<P STYLE="font-size:6pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>

<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">In certain investments, the team will take a board observer role to actively monitor the underlying credit. Responsibilities include analyzing
monthly, quarterly, and annual financial reports, participating in periodic update meetings or telephone calls, attending annual meetings, advisory board and informal meetings as appropriate, and making visits to the underlying portfolio companies
as warranted. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">This level of activity provides a breadth of information that enables the Company to better manage existing portfolio
investments, make intelligent new investment decisions, stay ahead of any potential issues, and generate attractive risk-adjusted returns. As such, the monitoring process is critical and helps the team make future investment decisions. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Valuation Process </I></B></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Board has
designated the Adviser as the Company&#8217;s valuation designee in accordance with Rule <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">2a-5</FONT> under the 1940 Act (the &#8220;<B>Valuation Designee</B>&#8221;) to value each investment in the Company&#8217;s
portfolio, subject to the oversight of the Board of Trustees. Investments for which market quotations are readily available are recorded at such market quotations, after evaluating whether such market quotations are representative of fair value.
With respect to investments for which market quotations are not readily available, it is expected that the Adviser, as the Valuation Designee, based on input of the Adviser&#8217;s valuation committee and one or more independent valuation firms that
are engaged at the direction of the Adviser&#8217;s valuation committee, will perform fair value determinations for such investments in good faith, in accordance with the Adviser&#8217;s valuation policy and procedures (the &#8220;<B>Valuation
Policy</B>&#8221;), adopted by and subject to the supervision of the Board of Trustees and pursuant to a consistently applied valuation process. See &#8220;<I>Item 9. Market Price of and Dividends on the Registrant&#8217;s Common Equity and Related
Shareholder Matters &#8212; Determination of NAV &#8211; Valuation of Portfolio Securities</I>.&#8221; </P>
 <p STYLE="margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt ; font-size:8pt">&nbsp;</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman" ALIGN="center">18 </P>

</DIV></Center>


<p style="margin-top:1em; margin-bottom:0em; page-break-before:always"> </p>
<HR SIZE="3" style="COLOR:#999999" WIDTH="100%" ALIGN="CENTER">
<h5 align="left" style="font-size:10pt;font-weight:bold"><a href="#toc">Table of Contents</a></h5>


<Center><DIV STYLE="width:8.5in" align="left">
 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Liquidating Investments </I></B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">In general, the Company expects its Middle Market Senior Loans to be repaid before their maturity through either a refinancing or
recapitalization event or a sale of the underlying portfolio company. The lead sponsor typically determines the timing and method of exit. The probability and timing of exit varies across the portfolio and is dependent on the type of
investment/instrument, the type of business involved and the views of the management team of the underlying portfolio company and the lead sponsor. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>There can be no assurance that the Company&#8217;s investment objective will be achieved or that losses will be avoided. There can be no
assurance that the Company&#8217;s yield target for investments will be achieved. </B></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Allocation of Investment Opportunities </I></B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Adams Street will provide investment management services to pooled investment vehicles, including the Company and other ASP Entities. See
&#8220;<I>Item 7. Certain Relationships and Related Transactions and Trustee Independence</I>.&#8221; </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Adams Street will share any
investment and sale opportunities with the Company and other ASP Entities in accordance with the Advisers Act and firm-wide allocation policies. Subject to the Advisers Act and as further set forth herein, certain other ASP Entities may receive
certain priority or other allocation rights with respect to certain investments, subject to various conditions set forth in such other ASP Entities&#8217; respective governing documents. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">In addition, as a BDC regulated under the 1940 Act, the Company will be subject to certain limitations relating to <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">co-investments</FONT> and joint transactions with affiliates, which, in certain circumstances, limit the Company&#8217;s ability to make investments or enter into other transactions alongside other ASP Entities. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Company, the Adviser and other related entities have been granted the <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">Co-Investment</FONT> Exemptive
Order. Pursuant to the <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">Co-Investment</FONT> Exemptive Order, the Company generally will be permitted to <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">co-invest</FONT> alongside certain of its affiliates if the Company and each
affiliate participating in the transaction acquire, or dispose of, as the case may be, the same class of securities, at the same time, for the same price and with the same conversion, financial reporting and registration rights, and generally with
substantially the same other terms. In addition, a &#8220;required majority&#8221; (as defined in Section&nbsp;57(o) of the 1940 Act) of the Independent Trustees will be required to make certain findings in connection with certain <FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">co-investment</FONT> transactions. The <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap">Co-Investment</FONT> Exemptive Order contains certain conditions that limit or restrict the Company&#8217;s ability to participate in such investment
opportunities. In such cases, the Company may participate in an investment to a lesser extent or, under certain circumstances, may not participate in the investment. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Managerial Assistance </I></B></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">As a BDC,
the Company will offer, and will be required to provide upon request, managerial assistance to its portfolio companies. This assistance could involve, among other things, monitoring the operations of the Company&#8217;s portfolio companies,
participating in portfolio company board and management meetings, consulting with and advising officers of portfolio companies and providing other organizational and financial guidance. The Company may also receive fees for these services. The
Administrator or an affiliate of the Administrator will provide, or arrange for the provision of, such managerial assistance on the Company&#8217;s behalf to portfolio companies that request this assistance. The Company may receive fees for these
services and reimburse the Administrator and/or an affiliate of the Administrator, as applicable, for its allocated costs in providing such assistance, subject to the review and approval by the Board of Trustees, including the Independent Trustees.
</P>
 <p STYLE="margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt ; font-size:8pt">&nbsp;</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman" ALIGN="center">19 </P>

</DIV></Center>


<p style="margin-top:1em; margin-bottom:0em; page-break-before:always"> </p>

 <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B>Investment Advisory Agreement </B></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>General </I></B></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The description below of
the Investment Advisory Agreement is only a summary and is not necessarily complete. The description set forth below is qualified in its entirety by reference to the Investment Advisory Agreement attached as an exhibit to this Registration
Statement. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Subject to the overall supervision of the Board of Trustees, the Adviser will manage the <FONT STYLE="white-space:nowrap"><FONT
STYLE="white-space:nowrap">day-to-day</FONT></FONT> operations of, and provide investment advisory and management services to, the Company pursuant to the Investment Advisory Agreement. Under the terms of the Investment Advisory Agreement, the
Adviser will be responsible for the following: </P> <P STYLE="font-size:6pt;margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt">&nbsp;</P>

investment objective, policies and restrictions, the 1940 Act, the Advisers Act and all other applicable federal and state law, and the Organizational Documents; </P></TD></TR></TABLE>

<TD ALIGN="left" VALIGN="top"> <P ALIGN="left" STYLE=" margin-top:0pt ; margin-bottom:0pt; font-family:Times New Roman; font-size:10pt">providing the Company with such other investment advisory, research and related services as the Company may, from
time to time, reasonably require for the investment and reinvestment of the Company&#8217;s assets. </P></TD></TR></TABLE> <P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Adviser&#8217;s
services under the Investment Advisory Agreement will not be exclusive, and it is free to furnish similar services to other entities, and it intends to do so, so long as it remains able to perform its obligations to the Company under the Investment
Advisory Agreement and Administration Agreement. </P> <P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><I>Term </I></P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">Unless earlier terminated as described below, the Investment Advisory Agreement will remain in effect for an initial term of two years, and
will remain in effect from year to year thereafter if approved annually by the Board of Trustees or by the holders of a Majority of the Outstanding Voting Securities (as defined below) and, in each case, a majority of the Independent Trustees. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:12pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The Investment Advisory Agreement will automatically terminate within the meaning of the 1940 Act and related SEC guidance and interpretations
in the event of its &#8220;assignment&#8221; (as such term is defined for purposes of Section&nbsp;15(a)(4) of the 1940 Act). In accordance with the 1940 Act, without payment of penalty, the Company may terminate the Investment Advisory Agreement
with the Adviser upon 60 days&#8217; written notice. The decision to terminate the agreement may be made by a majority of the Board of Trustees or the Shareholders holding a Majority of the Outstanding Voting Securities. &#8220;Majority of the
Outstanding Voting Securities&#8221; means the lesser of (i) 67% or more of the voting securities of the Company present or represented at a meeting if the holders of more than 50% of the outstanding voting securities of the Company are present or
represented by proxy or (ii)&nbsp;a majority of the outstanding voting securities of the Company. In addition, without payment of penalty, the Adviser may generally terminate the Investment Advisory Agreement upon 60 days&#8217; written notice. </P>
<P STYLE="margin-top:18pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman"><B><I>Compensation of the Adviser </I></B></P> <P STYLE="margin-top:6pt; margin-bottom:0pt; text-indent:4%; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman">The
Company will pay the Adviser investment advisory fees for its services under the Investment Advisory Agreement consisting of two components: a Management Fee and an Incentive Fee. The cost of both the Management Fee and the Incentive Fee will
ultimately be borne by the Shareholders. </P>
 <p STYLE="margin-top:0pt;margin-bottom:0pt ; font-size:8pt">&nbsp;</P> <P STYLE="margin-top:0pt; margin-bottom:0pt; font-size:10pt; font-family:Times New Roman" ALIGN="center">20 </P>

</DIV></Center>
